extracted.intended_audience: communication/media studies scholars and students; digital media researchers
extracted.subtask_short: Carey's ritual model for digital media
extracted.subtask_description: Apply James Carey’s ritual vs. transmission models of communication to natively digital artifacts, using the Brotherhood 2.0 YouTube project as a case study to identify what makes digital practices ritualistic. The page analyzes features that produce, maintain, repair, and transform shared cultural reality online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission model of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The transmission model describes communication as the transmission of signals or messages over distance for the purpose of control; commonly identified by terms such as 'imparting,' 'sending,' 'transmitting,' or 'giving information to others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value in this model lies in the information imparted (example: a news broadcast). Carey refines it as 'the transmission of signals or messages over distance for the purpose of control' (p.15). Use this criterion to evaluate instances where the primary function is information extension in space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual model of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The ritual model links communication to 'sharing,' 'participation,' 'association,' 'fellowship,' and 'the possession of a common faith' and views communication as symbolic work that produces and sustains a shared world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this view the important element is not the informational content but the act of receiving/participating and the role that practice plays in maintaining society over time (e.g., daily reading of a newspaper as forming a worldview). Use this to evaluate practices oriented toward sustaining shared beliefs and social bonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition/regular delivery as ritualizing mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine, scheduled delivery (e.g., daily publication or posting) creates ritual significance: the act of receiving media on a regular schedule maintains bonds and worldview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carey’s newspaper example and the vlogbrothers’ daily/alternating video schedule illustrate that the ritual value often lies in regularity rather than content. Check for consistent cadence (daily, weekly) and audience adherence to that schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform subscription/following features enable ritualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription or 'following' features that notify an audience when new content is posted support synchronous shared practices and help ritualize digital media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: YouTube's subscription notifications (and similar features on other platforms) inherently support ritualization by allowing many people to consume content on a shared timetable; evaluate platform affordances that facilitate collective temporal practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natively digital artifact criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'natively digital' artifact is something that could not effectively exist in its present form without digital technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to distinguish practices that rely on digital affordances (instant, cheap publishing; mass subscription; asynchronous mass interaction) from those that could be accomplished via pre-digital media (e.g., mailing videotapes). Brotherhood 2.0 is presented as natively digital because digital affordances made the practice practicable and scalable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience interactivity and comment-driven participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Active audience participation through comments and suggestions (e.g., proposing punishments, addressing creators directly) functions as part of the ritual dynamic and shapes content/behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include viewers suggesting punishments, addressing vloggers as friends, and co-producing norms; evaluate the degree and form of comment-mediated co-creation and role-taking (viewer as friend, participant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation and maintenance of a shared stock of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Ritual communities produce a publicly available stock of symbols (inside jokes, catchphrases, icons) that members use to recognize and inhabit the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify emergent symbolic vocabulary (e.g., 'DFTBA,' in-jokes, specialized forum names) and how these symbols are used to mark membership and sustain collective identity (Nerdfighteria as an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repairing reality through author–audience feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Repairing reality involves repurposing or modifying communal ideas; in digital contexts this can be dynamic because original creators participate in conversations and can address or alter community discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast Carey’s original notion (where authors may be unaware of repurposings) with Brotherhood 2.0 where John and Hank respond to audience-generated ideas in subsequent videos; evaluate responsiveness and dialogic repair as markers of ritual dynamism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation into physical community
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital rituals may transform virtual symbols and relations into physical gatherings and embodied sociality (e.g., meetups, conventions, fans wearing community symbols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidence of offline translation (organized gatherings, conventions, fans meeting and sustaining friendships), and symbolic artifacts (shirts, signage) that show the virtual community took on physical existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media-as-representation (news-as-drama) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a ritual view, media is not simply information but a dramatized representation of reality that invites audience participation by assuming social roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether media invites vicarious social role-taking (viewers act as friends, members) and whether content functions more as ritual/drama sustaining a worldview than as pure information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility/inclusion limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital ritual communities require Internet access and relevant technologies; lack of access excludes potential participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider socioeconomic and technical barriers when assessing the reach and representativeness of digital rituals; the paper notes Nerdfighteria is accessible only to the Internet-capable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive volume and information overload as a drawback
rubrics_metrics.description: The sheer volume of discourse generated by large digital communities can be overwhelming, which may impede individual participation and sense-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mechanisms (moderation, curated updates) that mitigate overload; Brotherhood 2.0 uses creators as moderators/distillers to surface salient ideas for less-engaged members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of founders/moderators in shaping and sustaining ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders or central figures often produce the original symbolic stock and function as moderators or distillers, shaping community norms and keeping the ritual coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who authors the initial symbols/tenets, how they moderate discourse, and how their ongoing presence influences community maintenance (John and Hank as 'rulers' of Nerdfighteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability depends on pre-existing conditions (fame, viral events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The success and scalability of a ritualized digital project may hinge on founders' prior audience, demographic targeting, and chance viral events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate context-specific enablers (author fame, initial audience composition, viral content) when judging whether a model can be copied; Brotherhood 2.0's growth is partially attributed to John’s existing teen readership and viral videos.
